object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier of goods or services to the organization, identified by a unique vendor number assigned at record creation.

source_references.excerpt: Dana: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master... Dana: Oh. Vendor number. Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The operational status of a vendor: draft (not yet approved), active (approved and transactable), or suspended (temporarily inactive).

source_references.excerpt: Dana: Draft, active, suspended... Mei: Collapsed into three, yes. Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.

object_types.name: SpendTier

source_references.excerpt: Dana: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold... Dana: I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.

object_types.name: RiskTier

ambiguities.description: Identification of Vendor: While vendor_number is the primary identifier, the business also uses other attributes (legal name, tax ID) for reference. The transcript mentions vendors with duplicate tax IDs and the system allows duplicate legal names (per the Meridian example). However, vendor_number is confirmed as unique. No ambiguity here -- vendor_number is clearly the identifier. However, the contact structure (see next ambiguity) introduces complexity.

Contact Management: The contact model is complex. The fact type 'Vendor operates in Region with Contact' combines a ternary relationship (Vendor-Region) with contact properties (name, email, phone). This raises the question: should ContactName, ContactEmail, and ContactPhone be modeled as separate entity types (ContactPerson with its own ID), or as value attributes on the ternary relationship? The current extraction models them as value types on the ternary fact. If contacts can be shared across vendors/regions or if they have independent identities, a refactoring would be needed.

source_references.excerpt: Mei: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number... Mei: Right. A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact. You cannot have two people both flagged primary for the same vendor in the same region -- the system rejects the second one.

ambiguities.description: Risk Tier Optionality: The transcript states that RiskTier is assigned by the review and that draft vendors have no review (hence no risk tier). However, the relationship 'Vendor has RiskTier' was extracted without a conditional mandatory constraint on active vendors. The model should clarify: is RiskTier optional for ALL vendors, or mandatory for active vendors only? Currently, the mandatory constraint is omitted from 'Vendor has RiskTier', which is correct (draft vendors have no risk tier). But this needs explicit documentation that only active vendors have a risk tier.

source_references.excerpt: Raj: Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier. Draft vendors don't have one... Raj: It's set by the review. A vendor with no review has no risk tier.

ambiguities.description: Current vs. Historical Risk Reviews: The transcript distinguishes between 'a vendor has several reviews over time' and 'one of them is the current signed-off one.' The current model includes a 'RiskReview is for Vendor' relationship but does not explicitly capture which review is the 'current' one. A separate fact type 'Vendor has CurrentRiskReview' might be needed, or an attribute on RiskReview (e.g., 'is current'). This is relevant to the constraint: 'Every active vendor has exactly one current signed-off review.' The model should clarify whether 'current' is modeled as state or derived.

source_references.excerpt: Raj: A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one. But one of them is the current signed-off one... Raj: ...You're right. Let me be precise. A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.

ambiguities.description: Vendor Status Transitions: The transcript reveals an unresolved policy issue: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended? Dana argues that orders already shipped should continue; Raj argues everything should halt. The facilitator explicitly parks this as undecided, noting no fourth status (e.g., 'run-off') has been agreed. The model captures only the three statuses (draft, active, suspended) and the creation-time control (PO can only be raised against active vendors). Post-suspension fulfillment behavior is NOT modeled because it is NOT agreed. This is correct but should be flagged as an open constraint.

source_references.excerpt: Raj: If we suspend a vendor -- their review lapses, or there's a breach, or they turn up on a sanctions list -- what happens to the purchase orders already in flight? My position is that everything halts immediately... Facilitator: Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided. Today's model captures three statuses and the creation-time control, and nothing about post-suspension fulfilment, because there is nothing agreed to capture.

ambiguities.description: Cardinality of Vendor Contacts per Region: The model captures 'a vendor in a region has exactly one primary contact.' But the reverse cardinality is ambiguous: can a single ContactName/Email/Phone be the primary contact for multiple vendors in the same region, or across regions? The transcript does not clarify this. If a contact person can serve multiple vendors (likely in practice), then the relationship should be remodeled. Currently, it is under-specified.

source_references.excerpt: Mei: Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region. So a vendor operating in EMEA and APAC has two primary contacts, one for each region... Mei: Right. A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact.

ambiguities.description: Terminology Ambiguity: 'Tier' is used for both spend-level (bronze/silver/gold) and risk-level (low/medium/high). While the transcript clarifies that these are two separate fields in the system, the ambiguous language persists in the organization ('high tier vendor' could mean high-spend or high-risk). The model uses distinct fact types (Vendor has SpendTier and Vendor has RiskTier) which resolves the ambiguity formally. However, users may still conflate the terms in conversation.

source_references.excerpt: Dana: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold... Raj: That's not the tier I use. I use low, medium, high... Mei: No. Two separate fields, different values, different owners. Procurement sets one, compliance sets the other.

ambiguities.description: Vendor Address Multiplicity: Dana mentions 'three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.' The current model includes a VendorAddress value type but does not capture the three distinct address roles. Should the model include separate fact types (Vendor has RemitToAddress, Vendor has ShipFromAddress, Vendor has LegalAddress)? The transcript does not provide enough detail on business rules for each, so they are not extracted. This is a potential extension.

source_references.excerpt: Dana: Legal name. Tax ID. Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong. Status. Tier. The contact.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID Non-Uniqueness: The transcript confirms that Tax ID is not a unique identifier due to parent-subsidiary structures and duplicate records. However, it remains unclear whether the system enforces any constraint on TaxID (e.g., whether duplicate tax IDs for different vendors are flagged, warned, or silently allowed). The model captures that TaxID is not an identifier, but the business rule for handling duplicates is not formally stated.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: And could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead? Dana: You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them... Facilitator: Noted, but out of scope for today. Tax ID isn't an identifier, vendor number is.

ambiguities.description: Informal Vendor Preferences: Mei maintains an unofficial spreadsheet with a 'preferred' column indicating which vendor to buy from if multiple can supply the same item. This is acknowledged as an ad hoc, undocumented rule with no formal decision process. The facilitator explicitly declines to model this because it is not a defined rule. However, if this practice should be formalized in the future, a fact type 'Vendor is Preferred for SupplyCategory' or similar would be needed.

source_references.excerpt: Mei: There's a column called 'preferred.' It means if two vendors can supply the same thing, buy from this one. It's not in the system anywhere. It's just my column... Mei: It's ad hoc. Don't model it.
